title: AI Media and Visual Repository
answer: Keynotes, conference talks, tutorials, podcasts with transcripts, and a diagram and image library.

reading.body:
The repository is a curated index of 18 items across three sections: 7 videos, 6 podcasts, and 5 images or diagrams. It is a catalog of pointers, not a store of content.

The pattern is editorial selection rather than aggregation. Each section states what it tracks and what it deliberately excludes: podcasts are listed by host, focus, and transcript availability rather than by live feed or download rank, and the image library points to freely usable diagrams and browser-based model explorers rather than hosting originals. The video section is organized around the moments where model and hardware announcements land, alongside course lectures and onboarding explainers.

For AI specifically, the video category is where compute news surfaces in public. Vendor keynotes are the venues where new accelerators and model generations are announced together, so a list of them is a list of the field's periodic hardware disclosures. The diagram library matters for a different reason: architecture diagrams and model explorers are how the physical and logical structure of training and inference gets communicated to people who will never read the papers.

What this does not tell the reader is anything about audience, reach, or quality. There are no view counts, no download figures, no dates on individual items, and no ranking within any section. The counts are small and the selection criteria are stated in prose, so the list reflects one editorial judgment about what is worth watching and reading, not a measurement of what the field actually consumes.
